case_info.scenario: An 84-year-old man with dementia presented to a dermatology clinic with a 1-week history of multiple dark violaceous nodules on his right leg and foot. The patient had no fevers, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, or leg pain or swelling, and no recent history of trauma. Nine months prior to presentation, he had been diagnosed with bullous pemphigoid, which was initially treated with oral prednisolone (40 mg daily for 1 week). His prednisolone dose was reduced by 10 mg per day each week to 10 mg daily, which he had been taking for 8 months. On presentation, his temperature was 36.7 °C (98.1 °F); blood pressure, 120/85 mm Hg; and heart rate, 92/min. Physical examination revealed multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on his right leg and 2 nodular masses with hemorrhagic crusts on his right foot (Figure 1). The right dorsalis pedis and popliteal artery pulses were normal to palpation. Laboratory testing revealed a normal complete blood cell count and normal creatinine and liver function test results; results of HIV antibody testing were negative.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.

case_info.caption: Multiple round, dark brown to violaceous-colored firm nodules on patient’s right leg and foot.
case_info.explanation: A. Evaluate skin biopsy histology and perform immunohistochemistry for human herpesvirus 8 antigen. The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that multiple dark-colored nodules on the lower extremity are characteristic of iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma in a patient treated with long-term daily corticosteroids. A wound culture (choice C) and antibiotics (choice D) are not recommended because there were no clinical signs or symptoms of infection. Arterial ultrasound (choice B) was not indicated because the clinical presentation with normal pedal pulses made peripheral artery disease unlikely. Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative neoplasm caused by Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus 8.1,2KSHV is primarily transmitted through saliva but can be acquired through receptive anal sex and, rarely, through organ transplant or blood transfusion.3After initial infection, KSHV exists in a latent state primarily in B lymphocytes and monocytes. Viral reactivation, which is associated with oncogenesis, may be precipitated by factors such as HIV or malaria infections and by immunosuppression.2Seroprevalence of KSHV varies worldwide, with a prevalence of more than 90% in Africa, 20% to 30% in the Mediterranean region, and less than 10% in the US, northern Europe, and Asia.1 Kaposi sarcoma is classified into 4 clinical variants. Classic Kaposi sarcoma affects males without HIV infection who are typically older than 70 years. Endemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in children and adults who are from endemic areas, such as sub-Saharan Africa. Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma affects patients treated with immunosuppressant medications. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HIV-induced immunosuppression.1,2 Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with distal lower extremity skin findings, including violaceous, dark brown, or reddish-blue macules, plaques, or nodules; these may be exophytic, ulcerative, or hemorrhagic.4Patients with severe Kaposi sarcoma may have more diffuse cutaneous manifestations or involvement of mucosa (eg, oral and throat), visceral organs (eg, respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts), and lymph nodes.4Although classic Kaposi sarcoma has a proposed staging system,5there is currently no standardized staging system for endemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.1,4 The differential diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma includes nodular melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, angiosarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis, and acroangiodermatitis of Mali, a reactive angiodysplasia associated with chronic venous insufficiency.4 Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma typically occurs in patients undergoing treatment with immunosuppressants after organ transplant or for immune-mediated diseases.6A study of US patients who received solid organ transplants from 1987 to 2014 and had no history of Kaposi sarcoma or HIV infection found that 163 of 244 964 (0.07%) developed Kaposi sarcoma.7Kaposi sarcoma has also been reported in patients taking long-term daily systemic corticosteroids to treat rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myasthenia gravis, nephrotic syndrome, and bullous pemphigoid.6,8,9 Although Kaposi sarcoma is often suspected based on characteristic skin lesions, the diagnosis should be confirmed by histological examination of a skin biopsy.1Typical findings on hematoxylin-eosin staining include spindle cells and dermis vascular proliferation. Immunohistochemical staining for KSHV antigens is also useful to diagnose Kaposi sarcoma.1 First-line treatment for iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma is withdrawal or dose reduction of immunosuppressants, which often results in partial or complete remission.6Tapering corticosteroid doses and transitioning patients to an alternative drug such as methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or sirolimus may also improve or resolve Kaposi sarcoma symptoms.6,8Additional treatment options for limited cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma include silver nitrate cauterization, intralesional chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical excision, and cryotherapy.6Systemic chemotherapy may be used for advanced-stage Kaposi sarcoma but is rarely curative.1,6 A skin biopsy of the patient’s right leg revealed atypical spindle cells and multiple dilated vascular spaces in the dermis; immunohistochemical staining was positive for human herpesvirus 8 antigen, which confirmed the diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (Figure 2). The dose of prednisolone was reduced to 5 mg daily. A computed tomography scan of the chest revealed multiple tiny nodules in the lung parenchyma bilaterally. After oncology specialists presented potential treatment options, including chemotherapy for probable disseminated pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma, the patient and his family opted for local radiation treatment. Two months after receiving 30-Gy radiation therapy 5 days per week for 3 weeks, his right lower extremity skin lesions had completely resolved. Three months later, a chest computed tomography scan revealed no change in the pulmonary nodules, and the right lower limb nodules had not recurred.
